overview: Aragon developed from a Pyrenean county into a kingdom and became the name of a wider crown linking distinct territories around the western Mediterranean. A common ruler did not make their laws, languages or institutions identical. The atlas’s 1000 to 1530 record spans that changing scale; examples from Barcelona belong to the later crown, not the early mountain kingdom.

periods.title: County and emerging kingdom
periods.summary: The atlas begins in 1000, before Ramiro I inherited the county of Aragon in 1035. Royal authority developed from that county; the dynastic connection with Barcelona came later.

periods.title: A composite Mediterranean crown
periods.summary: The 1137 pact linking Petronila and Ramon Berenguer IV laid the basis for the union. Later expansion created a crown of distinct territories.

periods.title: Shared monarchs, distinct institutions
periods.summary: The dynastic link with Castile did not immediately abolish the crown’s own administration. Its Council of Aragon was established in 1494.

items.text: Petronila was still a child when the 1137 betrothal agreement joined her future to Ramon Berenguer IV, count of Barcelona. Their wedding occurred in 1150. Keeping those dates separate avoids turning a dynastic arrangement made for a baby into an adult marriage ceremony.

The crown incorporated territories with different legal traditions. Aragon was both a particular kingdom and part of this larger monarchy. Calling every inhabitant “Aragonese” without explaining the scale would erase important Catalan, Valencian and other local identities.

James I commissioned a systematic legal compilation in 1247. The Getty’s Vidal Mayor, c. 1290 to 1310, preserves a Navarro-Aragonese translation of a lost Latin version. Law had to be organized, copied and understood through particular languages.

The Vidal Mayor deals with Christians of different ranks, Muslims and Jews. It reveals a society whose law distinguished status and religion. Sharing cities and markets did not mean enjoying identical legal rights.

The medieval Llibre de Sent Soví survives within a manuscript that also contains medical, grammatical, astrological and devotional texts. One volume could be a small collection of useful knowledge. Its recipes cannot simply be treated as the usual meals of every household.

The Council of Aragon, created in 1494, organized work through offices for different territories. Records of those offices show the continued complexity of the crown after the dynastic union with Castile. A shared monarch was not the same thing as a single uniform administration.

sections.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample

items.text: In Barcelona in 1401, municipal and church authorities united six hospitals into the Hospital de la Santa Creu. The new institution served poor people, orphans and the sick. Care was a civic and religious undertaking as well as a medical one.

Barcelona’s council also regulated and subsidized food supplies as part of its social policy. Feeding the city and supporting vulnerable residents helped authorities seek stability. Hospital buildings alone cannot tell us whether every person who needed assistance received it.

By about 1303, Barcelona had written rules against throwing dirty water and other waste into streets through windows or doorways. The existence of a ban suggests an unwelcome practice worth regulating, not evidence that every resident did it every day.

The ordinance’s Catalan begins “que ninguna persona no gos gitar en carrers”: “that no person dare throw into the streets.” This sample is quoted in the museum’s transcription. Some medieval writing was less about heroic battles and more about preventing an unpleasant surprise from upstairs.

The museum’s history identifies chamber pots and latrines as household solutions and notes medieval names for toilets such as necessaria. Those facilities varied by building. They should not be imagined as modern flushing toilets connected to one complete citywide system.

Part of Barcelona’s Rambla drainage channel was covered in 1364 to 1366. Public fountains also needed drains. Water supply and waste disposal required continuing labor and construction; the later crown’s impressive buildings rested on many less glamorous maintenance jobs.

ending.text: The 1530 atlas endpoint is not the end of Aragon. Its crown continued within the Spanish monarchy. Much later, the Nueva Planta changes dismantled key separate institutions: the 1707 decree affected Aragon and Valencia, and the Council of Aragon was suppressed that year. Regional communities, languages and identities continued.
